weeks.insight:
A tiny account with the comment velocity of one ten times its size.

The striking thing about week one isn't the follower counts — it's that 332 LinkedIn followers produced 73 comments, a 22% comment-to-follower ratio that far larger accounts rarely see. The '84% of vegans quit' post alone drew 41, and the reason looks structural rather than lucky: a counter-intuitive statistic followed by collective 'we' framing invites people to argue and confess rather than just tap a reaction. That's a depth signal, and depth is the harder thing to manufacture — reach tends to follow it more reliably than the reverse.

On Instagram the distribution question is already settled: Reels are 88.9% of views and static posts are close to invisible. Substack opens at 55.7%, comfortably above the ~40% a publisher reads as credible, though the list is still tiny at ~100.

The open question for the coming weeks: was the 41-comment post a repeatable format or a strong first swing? It's worth running the same structure deliberately on a different topic to find out — and worth keeping an eye on saves, which are low everywhere and are the metric that will eventually reveal whether people intend to come back.

weeks.insight:
One topic travelled across all three platforms at once — the first sign of a repeatable engine.

The week's real signal is Greece. The refugee-crisis idea showed up as a 3k-view Instagram Reel, a LinkedIn carousel, and a Substack essay (8.93% engagement, the highest of any issue so far) — the same thesis adapted three ways inside one week. That cross-platform coherence is exactly what a publisher looks for: not a single viral post but a person who can take an idea and work it across formats and audiences. Instagram is accelerating fastest (5,778 views vs 2,904), and external link taps doubled from 5 to 12 — the first evidence the Instagram-to-Substack funnel actually moves people. LinkedIn impressions settling to 4,512 from the week-one spike is just the launch bump normalising, not a decline to read into.

What's worth testing next: whether deliberately building each week around a single cross-platform theme — rather than posting per-platform in isolation — compounds that funnel. Greece did it by accident; the question is whether it works on purpose.

weeks.insight:
Reach went up and resonance went down — the two came apart this week.

Instagram added 19 followers, its biggest weekly jump yet, and the account was busy: eight posts, a witty 'aliens/cows' Reel, and a Gaza fundraiser carousel that travelled on cause rather than audience (92% of its interactions came from non-followers). But underneath the reach, depth thinned across the board — LinkedIn saves hit zero for the first time, comments fell to 4, Instagram saves were 1, and Substack posted its first net subscriber loss (-2), most likely older imported contacts disengaging. The interesting tension is that the busiest, highest-reach week produced the weakest depth so far. Reach and resonance, which moved together in week one, decoupled here.

That's worth sitting with, because for the book it's depth that carries more weight: a captive, returning readership beats a big number that doesn't come back. One experiment: on Instagram, try a single deliberately save-designed piece — a genuinely useful resource or list — and see whether a reach-heavy week can also bank depth rather than trade it away.

weeks.insight:
One talking-head Reel did more than the rest of the account combined.

The June 26 Reel — a plain face-to-camera talking head — pulled 956 views and 131 interactions, a 13.7% engagement rate that is exceptional for a 160-follower account and far beyond anything else this week. That single data point is the most useful thing to come out of the month: it hints the audience is beginning to form around Jacob-as-a-person, not just around topics or novelty. Instagram interactions jumped 145% and accounts engaged tripled to 147 — real depth, not just a view count. The counterweight is Substack, where no issue went out; so at the exact moment Instagram surged, the funnel had no fresh place to send people, and link taps fell to 1.

The obvious thing to test is repeatability — was 956 the format or the topic? But the more strategic question is sequencing: what happens if a strong talking-head Reel and a Substack issue land in the same week, so the attention has somewhere to convert?

weeks.insight:
Take the hero post away and Instagram reverts to its floor — which tells you where the floor actually is.

This was a week without a breakout, and the Instagram numbers are revealing precisely because of it: views, reach and interactions all fell back sharply (interactions 208 to 53) when the best post was a light AR-filter Reel (284 views) rather than a talking head. The read isn't 'a bad week' — it's that the account's reach still rides on individual hero posts rather than a rising baseline, so the absence of one exposes the true floor. Growth across all three platforms converged to a slow, symmetrical crawl (+4 LinkedIn, +4 Instagram, +2 Substack). The genuinely useful structural news is that Substack shipped on time again — the weekly engine is the part a publisher weights most, and it's turning.

Two things worth watching: whether novelty formats (filters, trends) quietly train the wrong audience — people who watch a gimmick once and never return — and whether a sustained run of talking-head Reels can lift the floor, so the account isn't hostage to whenever the next breakout happens to land.

weeks.insight:
The thing people watch and the thing that compounds are drifting apart.

Instagram rebounded the moment the talking-head format came back: the 8 July Reel (464 views, 32 interactions) was the best since June's standout, and reach and interactions recovered with it (interactions +34%, accounts engaged +21%). That's now two clean data points saying the same thing — this audience is forming around Jacob on camera, not around any particular topic. LinkedIn quietly turned too, impressions rising a second week to 885. The tension worth naming is that the channel people actually watch (Instagram) and the channel that would compound into a durable, portable readership (Substack) are pulling in opposite directions: the Substack list has held around 103 for three weeks and its open rate eased below 50% for the first time.

For the pitch, reach was never really the constraint — a readership that travels with you is. So the experiment that matters isn't another Reel for its own sake; it's conversion. Can a talking-head Reel be built explicitly to move a viewer onto the list — a specific promise, a concrete reason to subscribe now — and does the funnel actually carry them across? That's the one number worth trying to move next.

weeks.insight:
The list grew itself this week - no new post, no push, and it still added subscribers.

Every audience-size signal rose while every attention signal fell. Substack went to 108 (+5) - its first movement off 103 in three weeks - and it happened during a fortnight with no new issue and just 1 external link tap from Instagram. The new subscribers landed on 14, 15, 18 and 20 July, spread evenly through a silent week, which points away from any single post and toward passive discovery: the Substack network, recommendations, or the standing bio link. LinkedIn added 8 followers, its largest weekly gain since launch, on a week when impressions fell 40% to 530. Instagram added 5 despite its quietest week on record (views 486, -57%; reach 144, -78%; interactions 22, -69%).

Last week's read was that the number to move was conversion - whether a Reel could push viewers onto the list. This week quietly answers a different question: the list can move without any push at all. That's useful to know before a pitch, because it implies a floor of organic accumulation that doesn't depend on shipping every week. The flip side is that audience and attention decoupled - the content that normally does the accumulating barely ran, yet accumulation continued. So this week's growth isn't the product of this week's work; it's the residue of earlier posts plus platform mechanics.

The LinkedIn texture is worth a look. Its best-ever follower week rode on curation rather than original argument: the top posts were an amplification of Project Slingshot's campaign (193 impressions) and Sara Pascoe's poultry callout (122), while the one original - a systems-change essay on JBS scrapping its net-zero goal - drew zero engagement. Reactions-only again (12R/1C). Reposting other people's campaigns may be recruiting followers even while it does little for impressions or conversation - a different lever, with a different payoff, than the provocation format that's been off the menu for a while now.

Two things worth testing next. First, find out where the five subscribers actually came from - Substack's Growth/Traffic breakdown will say whether recommendations or the Instagram link is the engine. If it's the network, cross-recommendations become a compounding lever worth cultivating deliberately, and the weekly-cadence pressure eases: the list may not need a post every Wednesday to grow, only to stay warm. Second, the 30-day open rate keeps drifting down (47.47%, from 48.99%) even as the list grows - subscribers who arrive without reading anything are exactly the kind who dilute it. Whether list size and open rate start moving in opposite directions is the pair a publisher will read together, so it's the one to watch as the list expands.

weeks.insight:
Three weeks quiet, and the open-rate slide finally stopped.

The involuntary experiment continued: no new Substack issue for three weeks now, no new Instagram feed post for two, and this was the quietest week on record. Instagram views fell to 307 (-37% on an already-low 486), reach to 102, interactions to just 10; LinkedIn drew 513 impressions and reached 181 members. Everything the account watches shrank. Yet the audience counts still ticked up on all three platforms - LinkedIn 368 (+2), Instagram 178 (+3), Substack 110 (+2). That's the second straight week of audience size and attention pulling in opposite directions, but with two weeks of near-zero input behind it the upward drift now looks less like a lag from recent posts and more like a genuine organic floor.

The most interesting number is the one that didn't move. The Substack 30-day open rate held at exactly 47.47%, flat on last week, ending a four-week slide (55.1 -> 51.65 -> 48.99 -> 47.47 -> 47.47). Last week the worry was that a list growing through passive discovery would keep diluting the open rate as unengaged subscribers piled in. This week that didn't happen: +2 subscribers and the rate held. One week isn't a reversal, but the decline stalling while the list still grows is the better of the two outcomes that were on the table - and it's the pair a publisher reads together.

LinkedIn quietly ran a small natural experiment. Its one original this week - '62% of Americans are already willing to eat less meat... so let me be an optimist for a moment: the appetite is there' - was the first stat-anchored original in weeks. It uses the same raw ingredient as the launch post that drew 41 comments (a striking number up front) but frames it as optimism rather than blame. It got 1 engagement on 96 impressions. Not proof of anything, but a hint worth holding: the launch formula's pull may live in the 'we blame X, we blame Y' structure that implicates the reader, not simply in leading with a statistic. A positive stat gives people nothing to push against. It was otherwise a reactions-only week (6R/1C), and the curation lever that drove last week's record +8 followers wasn't repeated - follower growth duly settled back to +2.

Two things to watch. First, whenever the next Substack issue finally ships, watch what it does to the open rate: sending to a list that's been quiet for a month, part of it acquired passively, could either re-engage those readers or expose the dilution the flat rate is currently hiding. Second, Instagram is now the cleanest test running - two weeks coasting entirely on residual reach while followers keep creeping up. How long does that half-life last? The week the follower drift finally stalls will say how much of this growth was ever truly organic versus the fading echo of the June and early-July posts.
